examples.english: I wash my hands and then eat.

lookup_grammar.formation: Ichidan: drop る, add て (食べる → 食べて). Godan: depends on ending — う/つ/る → って; ぬ/ぶ/む → んで; く → いて; ぐ → いで; す → して. Irregular: する → して, くる → きて.
formation_notes: 行く is irregular: 行って (not いいて).
The て-form alone can also express a sequence: 朝起きて顔を洗う — 'get up in the morning and wash my face'.
lookup_grammar.meaning_detailed: The て-form is one of the most important verb forms in Japanese. It does not express a tense by itself but serves as the foundation for many other grammatical constructions: requests (-てください), progressive aspect (-ています), permission (-てもいい), prohibition (-てはいけない), sequence of actions, and many more. Mastering te-form conjugation is essential because it unlocks a large portion of Japanese grammar.
lookup_grammar.meaning_en: connecting form (basis for many compound constructions)

examples.english: This book is expensive and heavy.
examples.japanese: この本は高くて、重い。

examples.english: It's cold, so I don't want to go outside.
examples.japanese: 寒くて、外に出たくない。

search_grammar.formation: Drop final い, add くて: 高い → 高くて, おいしい → おいしくて, 寒い → 寒くて. Irregular: いい → よくて.
formation_notes: Cannot use で for i-adjectives — that is reserved for na-adj and nouns.
Exception: いい → よくて (matching the よく / よかった pattern).
Can chain multiple adjectives: 高くて、重くて、使いにくい ('expensive, heavy, and hard to use').
Causal usage: 寒くて、外に出たくない ('it's cold, so I don't want to go out').
search_grammar.meaning_detailed: 〜くて is the 'te-form' of i-adjectives, used to join clauses. It functions like the verb te-form: linking adjective phrases together ('X and Y') or giving a reason/cause ('X, so Y'). It is distinct from the 〜で form used for na-adjectives and nouns. Exception: いい → よくて.

examples.english: This room is quiet and clean.
examples.japanese: この部屋は静かで、きれいです。

examples.english: He is a student and 20 years old.
examples.japanese: 彼は学生で、20歳です。

examples.english: She is kind and cheerful.
examples.japanese: 彼女は親切で、明るい。

search_grammar.formation: na-adj root + で: 静か → 静かで, 元気 → 元気で. Noun + で: 学生 → 学生で, 会社員 → 会社員で.
formation_notes: Parallel to 〜くて for i-adjectives but with a different particle (で instead of くて).
Same で form for na-adjectives and nouns, reflecting the shared copula.
Can chain: 静かで、きれいで、広い ('quiet, clean, and spacious').
Causal usage: 彼は医者で、とても忙しい ('he is a doctor, so he's very busy').
search_grammar.meaning_detailed: The 〜で form is the copular 'te-form' used for na-adjectives and nouns. It joins clauses just like 〜くて for i-adjectives: 'X and Y' or 'X, so Y'. The same で form works for both na-adjectives and noun predicates, reflecting the underlying shared copula だ.
search_grammar.meaning_en: te-form of na-adjectives and nouns (joining / causal)

examples.english: If I had money, I'd want to buy a new computer.
examples.japanese: お金があったら、新しいパソコンを買いたいです。

search_grammar_en.formation: Verb-た + ら (食べた → 食べたら). い-adj: かった + ら (高かったら). Noun/な-adj: だった + ら (学生だったら).
formation_notes: Often used for past-tense 'when I did X, I discovered/found Y': 家に帰ったら、誰もいなかった ('when I got home, no one was there').
Can express future 'when/after': 東京に着いたら電話します ('I'll call when I arrive in Tokyo').
For definite future, the main clause can express will/intention/command/request. For past discovery, the main clause is a past event.
search_grammar_en.meaning_detailed: たら is the most versatile Japanese conditional. It attaches to the た-form of a verb (or the かった form of an い-adjective, だった of a noun/na-adjective) and expresses 'if/when X happens'. It can refer to either a single future event ('if X happens' / 'when X happens') or a past event where the speaker discovered something ('when I did X, Y happened'). It's generally the safest conditional to use when learners aren't sure which of たら/ば/と/なら to pick.

examples.english: If you study every day, you'll become skilled.
examples.japanese: 毎日勉強すれば、上手になります。

examples.english: If it's cheap, I'll buy it.
examples.japanese: 安ければ買います。

examples.english: If you go to bed early, you'll feel good in the morning.
examples.japanese: 早く寝れば、朝元気になります。

search_grammar_en.formation: Ichidan: drop る, add れば (食べる → 食べれば). Godan: u-row → e-row + ば (行く → 行けば, 飲む → 飲めば). い-adj: drop い, add ければ (高い → 高ければ). Negative: ～なければ. Irregular: する → すれば, くる → くれば.
formation_notes: ば is preferred for natural or generic conditions ('if you study, you'll understand' — 勉強すればわかる).
The main clause of a ば-sentence usually does not express commands, requests, or invitations. Use たら for those.
The exception is when the subjects differ or the condition is stative.
search_grammar_en.meaning_detailed: The ば-conditional expresses a hypothetical 'if' — typically generic conditions or natural laws. It tends to emphasize the condition itself and is common in proverbs, mathematical statements, and generic claims. For specific contingent plans, たら is more common.

examples.english: If you press this button, the door opens.
examples.japanese: このボタンを押すとドアが開きます。

examples.english: When spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom.
examples.japanese: 春になると桜が咲きます。

examples.english: If you turn right, you'll see the station.
examples.japanese: 右に曲がると、駅が見えます。

search_grammar_en.formation: Dictionary form of verb (or plain non-past of adjective/copula) + と
formation_notes: The main clause must be a natural/certain consequence. No commands/requests/invitations in the main clause.
Good for: natural laws, directions ('turn right and you'll see the bank'), habitual sequences.
Past tense usage expresses an unexpected discovery, similar to たら but with a nuance of automatic consequence.
search_grammar_en.meaning_detailed: The と-conditional expresses that one thing naturally or inevitably leads to another. It's used for natural laws, habitual consequences, and definite outcomes — 'when X happens, Y (always) happens'. It cannot be used with commands, requests, invitations, or volition in the main clause.

list_grammar_n4_head.formation: Ichidan: drop る, add られる. Godan: u-row → e-row + る. Irregular: する → できる, くる → こられる.
formation_notes: ら-less forms (食べれる, 見れる) are colloquial and widely used but grammatically nonstandard.
The object of a potential verb takes が (or sometimes を): 日本語が話せる ('can speak Japanese').
できる is a standalone word meaning 'can do'; it is the potential form of する and also used for general ability.
list_grammar_n4_head.meaning_detailed: The potential form expresses ability or possibility — 'can do X'. Ichidan verbs form it by dropping る and adding られる (食べる → 食べられる). Godan verbs change the final u-row kana to the corresponding e-row kana and add る (行く → 行ける, 話す → 話せる). In modern colloquial Japanese, ら is often dropped from ichidan potential forms (食べれる instead of 食べられる) — this is called ら抜き言葉 and is widely used but grammatically nonstandard. The irregular する becomes できる, and くる becomes こられる.
list_grammar_n4_head.meaning_en: can do / is able to do

list_grammar_n4_head.formation: Ichidan: drop る, add られる. Godan: u-row → a-row + れる. Irregular: する → される, くる → こられる.
formation_notes: The passive agent (the one who did the action) takes に: 先生に叱られた ('I was scolded by the teacher').
Suffering passive: even intransitive verbs can be used passively to express adversity (雨に降られる, 友達に来られる).
list_grammar_n4_head.meaning_detailed: The passive form expresses that the subject receives an action. Ichidan verbs form it by dropping る and adding られる. Godan verbs change the u-row kana to the a-row and add れる. Note that ichidan passive and potential forms are homophones (食べられる can mean 'can eat' or 'is eaten'). Japanese also has a distinctive use of passive to express that something bad or unwanted happened to the speaker — the 'suffering passive' (私は雨に降られた — 'I got rained on').
list_grammar_n4_head.meaning_en: is done (passive); also expresses adversity / indirect affect
